Quantification of one or more antibodies to the superantigen toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) produced by Staphylococcus aureus in a sample.
Quantification of  one or more antibodies to the hepatitis B virus anitgen in a sample.
A microfluidics-free single-cell RNA sequencing method that uses particle-templated emulsification to encapsulate and barcode individual cells in uniform droplet emulsions.
A benchtop single-cell RNA sequencing kit developed by Scipio Bioscience that uses hydrogel technology for instrument-free single-cell analysis.

An end-to-end platform for high-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing, designed to enable efficient and high-density capture, stabilization, storage, and analysis of transcriptomic profiles from individual cells. Developed by Honeycomb Biotechnologies in collaboration with Revvity, the solution integrates sample collection, cell capture, and sample stabilization within a single device, eliminating the need for complex instrumentation at the collection site.

A prediction outputted by the ensemble model leveraging both liver and pancreas MRIs, which estimates how old the abdominal organs and tissues appear biologically, as opposed to chronological age (time since birth).
A reported family history of diabetes in one or more family members.
A reported family history of heart disease in one or more family members.
A reported family history of high blood pressure in one or more family members.

A phenotype representing systemic inflammatory status, often operationalized in population studies as a binary trait defined by elevated inflammatory biomarkers such as white blood cell count and/or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein.
A method that utilizes barcoded beads to capture mRNA for sequencing and preserves the spatial context of cells for downstream analysis.

A bead-based spatial transcriptomics kit designed with 3 mm x 3 mm tiles that enable high-resolution, whole transcriptome spatial mapping of fresh frozen tissue sections at single-cell (10 μm) resolution, using spatially-indexed beads for RNA capture and compatible with standard sequencing workflows.

A bead-based spatial transcriptomics kit designed with 10 mm x 10 mm tiles that enable high-resolution, whole transcriptome spatial mapping of fresh frozen tissue sections at single-cell (10 μm) resolution, using spatially-indexed beads for RNA capture and compatible with standard sequencing workflows.

CUT&Tag stands for cleavage under targets and tagmentation and is a chromatin profiling method that uses antibody-targeted tagmentation to map the locations of specific proteins, histone modifications, or transcription factors on DNA. The method involves binding an antibody to the protein target of interest, then recruiting protein A-Tn5 transposase fusion protein which cleaves and inserts sequencing adapters into DNA adjacent to the antibody-bound target (tagmentation). The tagmented DNA fragments are then amplified and sequenced using high-throughput sequencing. CUT&Tag offers improved signal-to-noise ratios and requires fewer cells compared to ChIP-seq.

The Ultima UG100 is a high-throughput sequencing machine developed by Ultima Genomics. It is designed for large scale sequencing projects including single cell RNA sequencing and human genome sequencing. This system uses emulsion-based PCR amplification.
The PacBio Revio is a high-throughput, long-read sequencing machine developed by Pacific Biosciences. This system is a single-molecule based sequencing technology that can read base modifications.
The Onso system is a high-throughput benchtop short-read DNA sequencing machine developed by PacBio.
The Element Aviti is a high-throughput benchtop sequencing machine developed by Element. This system uses rolling circle amplification instead of PCR to generate clusters.
The Element Aviti LT is a low- and medium-throughput benchtop sequencing machine developed by Element. This system has a lower through-put than the Aviti.

The Illumina MiSeq i100 is a high-throughput benchtop sequencing machine developed by Illumina. Its primary applications include small whole-genome sequencing, targeted sequencing of a set of genes or gene regions, 16S metagenomic sequencing and checking sample pooling prior to large scale sequencing.

A quantitative measurement technique derived from diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging that characterizes the three-dimensional diffusion of water molecules within biological tissues. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) calculates multiple parameters including fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity to assess tissue microstructure, white matter integrity, and cellular organization in various organs and tissues.

A quantitative parameter derived from diffusion tensor imaging that measures the average magnitude of water molecule diffusion across all spatial directions within a tissue. Mean diffusivity (MD) is calculated as the mean of the three eigenvalues of the diffusion tensor and provides information about tissue microstructure, cellularity, and integrity. This measurement can be applied to various biological tissues including brain, kidney, skeletal muscle, and other organs.

A quantitative parameter derived from diffusion tensor imaging that measures water molecule diffusion parallel to the principal direction of the diffusion tensor. Axial diffusivity (AD or AxD) represents the largest eigenvalue (λ1) of the diffusion tensor and provides information about axonal integrity and tissue microstructure. This measurement can be applied to various biological tissues including brain white matter, skeletal muscle, kidney, and other organs.

A quantitative parameter derived from diffusion tensor imaging that measures water molecule diffusion perpendicular to the principal direction of the diffusion tensor. Radial diffusivity (RD) is calculated as the average of the second and third eigenvalues ((λ2 + λ3)/2) of the diffusion tensor and provides information about myelin integrity and tissue microstructure. This measurement can be applied to various biological tissues including brain white matter, skeletal muscle, kidney, and other organs.

A measurement assessing the severity of symptoms experienced during menstruation, including but not limited to pain, cramping, discomfort, and other physical or psychological manifestations that may affect quality of life.

A nutritional deficiency disease resulting from inadequate selenium levels in the body, which can lead to impaired function of selenoproteins essential for antioxidant defense and thyroid hormone metabolism.

A sex-specific mathematical index calculated from body mass index, waist circumference, triglycerides, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol that estimates visceral adipose tissue function and serves as an indicator of adipose tissue dysfunction and cardiometabolic risk.

A visceral adiposity index value that has been statistically adjusted for body mass index to account for overall adiposity, allowing assessment of visceral adipose tissue dysfunction independent of general obesity status.

A calculated anthropometric index derived from hip circumference and height using the formula ((hip circumference in cm) / (height in m)^1.5) - 18, which directly estimates percent body fat for adult men and women without requiring body weight measurement.

A body adiposity index value that has been statistically adjusted for body mass index, enabling the assessment of the relationship between hip circumference-derived adiposity and health outcomes independent of overall body weight status.
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL).
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to high-density lipoproteins (HDL).
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to low-density lipoproteins (LDL).
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to very large VLDL.
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to small VLDL.
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to medium HDL.
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to small HDL.
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to small LDL.
Quantification of cholesterol esters contained in or bound to intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL).
A lipoprotein concentration assay that measures the concentration of very large very low-density lipoprotein particles in a specimen.
A lipoprotein concentration assay that measures the concentration of very large high-density lipoprotein particles in a specimen.
A lipoprotein concentration assay that measures the concentration of medium high-density lipoprotein particles in a specimen.
A lipoprotein concentration assay that measures the concentration of small high-density lipoprotein particles in a specimen.
The age at which an individual is diagnosed with high-grade serous ovarian cancer.

A bronchiectasis inflammatory endotype characterized by excessive neutrophil-driven airway inflammation with elevated levels of neutrophil-associated mediators including neutrophil elastase (NE), IL-8, and TNF-alpha. This is the most common inflammatory phenotype of bronchiectasis, strongly associated with chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, severe disease, frequent exacerbations, and poor prognosis.

A bronchiectasis inflammatory endotype characterized by elevated blood eosinophils (≥300 cells/μL) or sputum eosinophils (≥3%), associated with type 2 (Th2) inflammation, elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), and IL-5/IL-13 signaling. This phenotype affects approximately 20% of patients with bronchiectasis and may be responsive to inhaled corticosteroids and biologic agents targeting Th2 pathways.

A bronchiectasis inflammatory endotype characterized by concurrent neutrophilic and eosinophilic (type 2/Th2) inflammation, with co-expression of neutrophil-associated markers (neutrophil elastase, IL-8) and eosinophilic markers (IL-5, IL-13, FeNO). This endotype represents a distinct biological subgroup associated with increased exacerbation risk and potential responsiveness to combined therapeutic strategies.

A bronchiectasis inflammatory endotype characterized by low levels of both neutrophils (<60%) and eosinophils (<3%) in the sputum, with reduced concentrations of inflammatory mediators including IL-8 and IL-13. This phenotype is associated with milder disease presentation on imaging and lower exacerbation burden, though it remains less well-characterized than other bronchiectasis endotypes.

A bronchiectasis endotype characterized by cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) dysfunction that does not meet full diagnostic criteria for cystic fibrosis, typically presenting with elevated sweat chloride concentration (intermediate range 30-59 mmol/L), mucociliary clearance defects, and susceptibility to nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary infection. Patients may carry heterozygous CFTR mutations or have reduced CFTR function without detectable mutations, and may be candidates for CFTR modulator therapy.

A bronchiectasis endotype characterized by ciliary dysfunction that does not meet full diagnostic criteria for primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), typically presenting with abnormally low nasal nitric oxide levels, ciliary beat frequency abnormalities, and impaired mucociliary clearance. This endotype represents a spectrum of ciliopathy-associated bronchiectasis distinct from classical PCD.

A bronchiectasis endotype associated with heritable connective tissue disorder features, characterized by a tall asthenic morphotype with high rates of scoliosis, pectus excavatum, mitral valve prolapse, and dural ectasia. This endotype is associated with susceptibility to pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacterial infection and may involve genetic variation in connective tissue and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta)-related pathway genes.

A bronchiectasis endotype characterized by underlying immune deficiency, presenting with impaired systemic immunity and increased susceptibility to mycobacterial infection, particularly nontuberculous mycobacteria. This endotype encompasses a spectrum of primary and acquired immunodeficiencies that predispose to chronic airway infection and bronchiectatic disease.

An assay that evaluates the biological function or activity of a gene, protein, or variant by measuring a phenotypic or molecular readout in a yeast cell system, typically through growth, morphology, stress sensitivity, reporter expression, or related outputs.

A physiological or behavioral change that occurs in response to amphetamine, a central nervous system stimulant that acts primarily by increasing the release and blocking the reuptake of monoamine neurotransmitters including dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin.

A physiological or immunological change that occurs in response to penicillin, a beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis. Response may include therapeutic efficacy, allergic or hypersensitivity reactions, or other adverse effects.

A physiological or therapeutic change that occurs in response to tocilizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to both soluble and membrane-bound interleukin-6 receptors (IL-6R), thereby inhibiting IL-6-mediated signaling and inflammatory responses.

A physiological or therapeutic change that occurs in response to sunitinib, a multi-targeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor that inhibits VEGFR, PDGFR, c-KIT, RET, and FLT3 signaling pathways, affecting tumor angiogenesis and proliferation.

A physiological or therapeutic change that occurs in response to nintedanib, a triple angiokinase inhibitor that blocks VEGFR, FGFR, and PDGFR tyrosine kinases, inhibiting angiogenesis and fibrotic processes.

A physiological or therapeutic change that occurs in response to vandetanib, a multi-kinase inhibitor that targets VEGFR, EGFR, and RET tyrosine kinases, primarily used in the treatment of medullary thyroid cancer.

A physiological or therapeutic change that occurs in response to vemurafenib, a selective BRAF kinase inhibitor that targets the BRAF V600E mutation, primarily used in the treatment of BRAF-mutant melanoma.

A physiological or therapeutic change that occurs in response to mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid), an anti-inflammatory drug that acts locally in the gastrointestinal tract, primarily used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease including ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.

A physiological or pathological response to exposure to zonisamide, a benzisoxazole sulfonamide anticonvulsant drug. This response encompasses changes in motor symptoms, wearing-off effects, and therapeutic outcomes observed following zonisamide administration in patients with Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations.

A physiological or pathological response to exposure to a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist. GLP-1 receptor agonists are a class of incretin-mimetic drugs that bind to and activate the GLP-1 receptor, stimulating glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppressing glucagon release, delaying gastric emptying, and promoting satiety. This response encompasses glycemic control outcomes including HbA1c reduction, body weight changes, and other metabolic effects observed following GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment.

A physiological or pathological response to exposure to a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor. DPP-4 inhibitors are a class of oral antidiabetic drugs that inhibit the enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase-4, thereby increasing the half-life of endogenous incretin hormones. This response encompasses both therapeutic outcomes such as glycemic control and adverse effects including drug-induced bullous pemphigoid.
The volume of a specimen that is taken or allocated for the purpose of conducting one or more assays or measurements.
The volume of a buffer.

DNBSEQ-T7 is a high-throughput next-generation sequencing platform launched in 2019 by MGI Tech Co., Ltd. (a subsidiary of BGI Group), based on DNBSEQ technology that employs DNA Nanoball (DNB) amplification — whereby circularised DNA templates are replicated by rolling-circle amplification into compact nanoballs and loaded onto patterned nanoarrays — and combinatorial probe-anchor synthesis (cPAS) for massively parallel sequencing. The platform is designed for large-scale genomic projects and offers high throughput comparable to the Illumina NovaSeq 6000, with demonstrated applications in whole-genome sequencing, whole-exome sequencing, and bisulfite sequencing.

Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression is a probe-based, whole-transcriptome spatial gene expression assay that captures mRNA at single-cell-scale resolution using continuous 2 µm capture features (~11 million features across a 6.5 × 6.5 mm capture area), compatible with formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE), freshly frozen, and fixed frozen tissue sections.

CosMx SMI is a high-plex in situ analysis platform to provide spatial multiomics with formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and fresh frozen (FF) tissue samples at cellular and subcellular resolution.
The reproductive years when a person has regular menstrual periods, without experiencing any symptoms of perimenopause or menopause.

The transitional phase before menopause, characterized by declining and fluctuating estrogen levels and associated symptoms such as irregular menstrual periods, hot flashes, night sweats, and mood changes. This phase typically begins several years before menopause and ends with the last menstrual period.
The activity or process of determining, analyzing, or predicting all or part of an organism's phenotype.
An hTERT-immortalized cell line derived from human thoracic aorta.
A transfection that describes the means by which nucleic acid molecules (DNA or RNA) are physically or chemically introduced into target cells.
Method by which nucleic acids are delivered or engineered into a cell.
A nucleic acid delivery method that uses viral vectors to introduce nucleic acid cargo into target cells by exploiting viral mechanisms of cell entry and genome delivery.
Viral-based transfection, or more specifically known as transduction, involves using a viral vector to carry a specific nucleic acid sequence into a host cell.
A viral transduction method in which the viral nucleic acid cargo stably integrates into the host cell genome, enabling heritable and long-term transgene expression.
Stable transfection ensures long-term expression of a transgene by integrating the introduced DNA into the host genome, therefore, maintaining the expression even after replication.

A stable viral transduction method that uses lentiviral vectors, derived from lentiviruses such as HIV-1, to deliver nucleic acid cargo into both dividing and non-dividing cells via stable integration into the host chromosomal DNA.
Stable transfection method involving the transgene introduction into the cells of interest using engineered lentiviral particles.

A stable viral transduction method that uses retroviral vectors, derived from oncoretroviruses such as gammaretroviruses, to deliver nucleic acid cargo into dividing cells via stable integration of the retroviral genome into the host chromosomal DNA.
Stable transfection method involving the transgene introduction into the cells of interest using engineered retroviral particles.

A viral transduction method in which the viral nucleic acid cargo enters target cells but does not stably integrate into the host genome, resulting in transient transgene expression that is lost upon cell division.
Transient transfection is the introduction of foreign nucleic acids into eukaryotic cells resulting in temporary expression of the introduced genes, without integration into the host genome.

A transient viral transduction method that uses adenoviral vectors to deliver nucleic acid cargo into target cells, where the viral DNA persists as an episomal element without integrating into the host genome.

Transient transfection method involving the transgene introduction into the cells of interest using engineered adenoviral particles. Adenoviral particles can transduce both replicating and non-dividing cells. Adenoviral DNA does not integrate into the host genome, but rather, resides episomally in the host nucleus.

A transient viral transduction method that uses adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors to deliver nucleic acid cargo into target cells, where the vector DNA predominantly persists as episomal concatemers with minimal integration into the host genome.

Transient transfection method involving the transgene introduction into the cells of interest using engineered adeno-associated virus (AAV) particles. AAV particles can transduce both replicating and non-dividing cells. Engineered AAV DNA does not integrate into the host genome, but rather, resides episomally in the host nucleus. In comparison to adenoviral vectors, AAVs have low immunogenicity and cytotoxicity.

A transient viral transduction method that uses herpesviral vectors, derived from herpesviruses such as herpes simplex virus (HSV), to deliver nucleic acid cargo into target cells, particularly neurons, without permanent integration into the host genome.

Transient transfection method involving the transgene introduction into the cells of interest using engineered Herpes simplex virus (HSV) particles. HSV particles can transduce both replicating and non-dividing cells. Engineered HSV DNA does not integrate into the host genome, but rather, resides episomally in the host nucleus. HSV vectors have comparatively large transgene capacity (approx. 30kB) and have low immunogenicity.
A nucleic acid delivery method that uses physical or chemical approaches other than viral vectors to introduce nucleic acids into target cells.

Non-viral transfection methods rely on physical or chemical means to introduce nucleic acids into cells without the use of viral vectors. Non-viral transfection methods are often preferred for their safety and ease of use, as they do not involve the complexities and potential risks associated with viral vectors, at the cost of lower transfection efficiency and specificity.
A non-viral transfection method in which brief, high-voltage electrical pulses are applied to cells, transiently permeabilizing the plasma membrane to allow uptake of nucleic acids into the cell.
Electroporation is the process of using an electric pulse to introduce DNA into cells by creating temporary pores in the cell membrane, allowing for efficient gene delivery.

A non-viral transfection method that combines cell-type-specific electrical parameters and proprietary reagents to deliver nucleic acids directly into the nucleus of cells, including difficult-to-transfect primary and non-dividing cells.
Nucleofection is a type of specialized electroporation which is designed to deliver genetic material directly to the nuclei of cells.

A non-viral transfection method in which cationic lipid formulations spontaneously form complexes with negatively charged nucleic acids and fuse with the cell membrane to deliver the nucleic acid cargo into target cells.

Lipofection is a liposome-based transfection technique whereby the nucleic acid is encapsulated within a phospholipid vesicle that can either directly fuse with cell membranes or be endocytosed by a cell, allowing delivery of the genetic material to the cell.
A non-viral transfection method in which nanoparticles, such as polymeric, inorganic, or lipid nanoparticles, are used as carriers to encapsulate and deliver nucleic acid cargo into target cells.

Nanoparticle-mediated transfection is a method for delivering genetic material into cells using small (<100 nm in diameter) nanoparticles, which can encapsulate genetic material and facilitate its entry into the cell. The nanoparticles can be engineered to enhance cellular specificity, protect the genetic material from degradation, and release it once inside the cell.
A non-viral transfection method in which a fine glass capillary needle is used under microscopic guidance to directly inject nucleic acids or other macromolecules into individual cells.

Microinjection is a method that enables introduction of exogenous genetic material (or other substances, such as proteins) directly into the cytoplasm or nucleus of individual cells using a micrometer-diameter pipette by piercing the cell and/or nuclear membrane under visual control.
A non-viral transfection method in which a focused laser beam creates transient pores in the cell membrane, enabling the entry of nucleic acids into the cell without mechanical penetration.
Nucleic acid delivery method which involves short low-power bursts of laser beam to create transient pores in the cell membrane to allow entry of genetic material to the cell.
A non-viral transfection method that uses ultrasound waves, often combined with microbubbles, to transiently permeabilize cell membranes and facilitate cellular uptake of nucleic acids.

Sonoporation is a technique for delivering genetic material into cells using sonication. In this process, externally applied acoustic pressure waves create temporary pores in the cell membrane, enabling the genetic material to enter the cell.

A property of a transfected nucleic acid that describes the mode by which the delivered nucleic acid persists in the host cell in relation to the host genome, including integration into chromosomal DNA or episomal persistence.
The state of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) being integrated into a host genome, often as a result of viral infection or genetic engineering.

A nucleic acid integration state in which the delivered nucleic acid inserts into the host genome at non-specific, random chromosomal locations, as typically occurs with retroviral and lentiviral vectors.
Random locus integration refers to the process where an exogenous genetic material is inserted into the host genome at an arbitrary, rather than a specific, location.

A nucleic acid integration state in which the delivered nucleic acid is directed to integrate at a specific, pre-defined chromosomal locus using site-specific recombination systems or precision genome editing tools.

Targeted locus integration refers to the process where an exogenous genetic material is inserted into the host genome at specifically pre-determined location using cell's homology-directed repair mechanisms. In contrast to the random locus integration approach, this minimises the risk of insertional mutagenesis and ensures more consistent transgene expression.

A nucleic acid integration state in which the delivered nucleic acid sequence replaces an endogenous sequence at the native genomic locus via homology-directed repair, preserving the natural chromosomal context.

Native locus replacement refers to the process where the exogenously introduced genetic material replaces the host's native genomic sequence. This is achieved by introducing double-stranded DNA breaks in the host genome using gene editing tools, such as CRISPR/Cas9 or TALENS, together with template DNA (often a corrected or modified version of the gene) flanked by homology arms to promote the sequence incorporation into the host's genome at a native locus by means of homology-directed repair.

A nucleic acid integration state in which the delivered nucleic acid persists episomally in the host cell without integration into the chromosomal DNA, resulting in transient or non-heritable transgene expression.

Non-integrative transgene expression refers to the process where the foreign genetic material is expressed without being permanently incorporated into the host's genome. Instead, the transgene exists in the cell as a separate entity, usually in the form of an episome, plasmid, or mRNA.
The 10x probe-based assay that uses a 8bp probe barcode for sample identification.

The 10x probe-based assay where probe pairs targeting the whole transcriptome are used in conjunction with sample specific probe barcodes, allowing for singleplexed or multiplexed experiments, with a recommended 8,000 cells targeted per probe barcode.

The 10x probe-based assay where probe pairs targeting the whole transcriptome are used in conjunction with sample specific probe barcodes, allowing for singleplexed or multiplexed experiments. GEM-X includes a redesigned microfluidic chip with a recommended 20,000 cells targeted per probe barcode.
The 10x probe-based assay that introduces a scalable plate-based multiplexing system using a 10bp sample barcode for sample identification and allows for up to 384 samples per week.
A region of the whole organism without well-defined compartmental boundaries.

Any process that results in a change in state or activity of a cell or an organism (in terms of movement, secretion, enzyme production, gene expression, etc.) as a result of treatment with obinutuzumab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used to treat B-cell malignancies and other B-cell–mediated disorders.

Any process that results in a change in state or activity of a cell or an organism (in terms of movement, secretion, enzyme production, gene expression, etc.) as a result of treatment with ofatumumab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used to treat B-cell malignancies and other B-cell–mediated disorders.

Any process that results in a change in state or activity of a cell or an organism (in terms of movement, secretion, enzyme production, gene expression, etc.) as a result of treatment with rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used to treat B-cell malignancies and other B-cell–mediated disorders.
A protocol which provides instructions on the process of creating visual representations of specimens or phenomena.

A protocol that specifies the steps and conditions for fixation of biological material (e.g. cells or tissues), using chemical and/or physical methods to preserve structural and molecular features and limit post-collection degradation (including autolysis/putrefaction) for downstream analysis.

A measurement of the duration for which cells or cell membranes are kept in a permeabilized state to enable increased transmembrane passage of otherwise poorly permeant molecules (for example, dyes, antibodies, or nucleic acids).

Quantification of the amount of esterified desmosterol in a sample. Desmosterol (also known as 24-dehydrocholesterol, CHEBI:17737) is a zoosterol and the immediate precursor to cholesterol in the Bloch pathway of de novo cholesterol biosynthesis, where it is converted to cholesterol by the enzyme DHCR24 (delta-24-sterol reductase).

Quantification of the amount of free (non-esterified) desmosterol in a sample. Desmosterol (also known as 24-dehydrocholesterol, CHEBI:17737) is a zoosterol and the immediate precursor to cholesterol in the Bloch pathway of de novo cholesterol biosynthesis, where it is converted to cholesterol by the enzyme DHCR24 (delta-24-sterol reductase).

Quantification of the total amount of desmosterol (sum of free and esterified forms) in a sample. Desmosterol (also known as 24-dehydrocholesterol, CHEBI:17737) is a zoosterol and the immediate precursor to cholesterol in the Bloch pathway of de novo cholesterol biosynthesis, where it is converted to cholesterol by the enzyme DHCR24 (delta-24-sterol reductase).
A string used to identify a sample.
Myocardial strain refers to the measurement of heart muscle deformation, or its shortening, thickening, and lengthening, using imaging techniques like echocardiography.
A measurement of the distance spanning the widest transverse diameter of the fetal skull, between the outer or inner tables of the two parietal bones, typically obtained by ultrasound.

A semi-quantitative prenatal ultrasound measurement of amniotic fluid volume, calculated as the sum of the deepest vertical pocket of amniotic fluid measured in each of the four quadrants of the uterus.
The rate of contraction of the fetal heart, typically expressed as the number of fetal cardiac beats per minute.
An assay that measures the abundance or distribution of one or more molecular analytes, such as RNA or proteins, while preserving their spatial localization within cells or tissues.

A spatial molecular profiling assay that simultaneously maps mRNA transcripts and protein expression within intact tissue sections using microfluidic co-delivery of DNA barcodes. Spatially indexed barcodes are deposited in a deterministic grid pattern onto the tissue, capturing both RNA and antibody-DNA conjugates, which are subsequently sequenced to yield co-registered transcriptomic and proteomic profiles. This approach provides paired spatial gene expression and protein abundance data at near-cellular, pixel resolution.
A mass spectrometry assay that couples ambient ionization to mass spectrometry (MS) for chemical analysis of samples at atmospheric conditions.

An imaging assay that selectively amplifies Raman signals from specific molecular bonds (e.g., C–H, C=C) using pulsed laser excitation. Improvements to standard SRS—such as lock-in detection, signal amplification, or optimized laser configurations—increase sensitivity and spatial resolution, enabling detection of low-abundance biomolecules. This technique provides non-destructive, quantitative maps of lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, and other chemical species at subcellular resolution.

A spatial molecular profiling assay that enables non-destructive, multiplexed profiling of RNA and protein from user-selected regions of interest (ROIs) within intact tissue sections. For RNA, tiled in situ hybridization probe sets targeting 1000s of transcripts are conjugated to photocleavable DNA indexing oligonucleotides; for protein, antibodies specific to up to 96 protein targets are similarly conjugated to photocleavable oligo tags. After ROI selection, UV illumination releases the oligo tags from the illuminated areas, which are collected and quantified on the NanoString nCounter system. This approach supports targeted spatial gene expression and protein profiling from defined tissue regions.

Individual-nucleotide resolution UV-Crosslinking and Affinity Purification (iCLAP) is a high-stringency molecular technique that maps the RNA-binding sites of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) at single-nucleotide resolution. RNA–protein complexes are covalently crosslinked by UV irradiation, followed by stringent affinity purification of the target RBP and sequencing of the co-purified RNA fragments. The resulting data reveals the positions where an RBP contacts its RNA targets.

A spatial transcriptomics assay that maps whole-transcriptome gene expression within intact tissue sections at capture-spot resolution, ranging from multi-cellular to near single-cell depending on array configuration. Tissue sections are placed on spatially barcoded capture arrays; RNA transcripts bind to capture probes and are sequenced together with their spatial barcodes to reconstruct a spatially resolved gene expression map. This approach preserves spatial context while enabling unbiased, genome-wide profiling of gene expression across tissue regions.

A mass spectrometry assay in which analytes co-crystallized with a chemical matrix are ionized by a pulsed laser, generating predominantly singly charged ions that are detected by mass-to-charge ratio; when performed as raster-scanned imaging (MALDI-MSI), it generates spatially resolved molecular maps of proteins, peptides, lipids or metabolites directly from tissue sections.
An extraction protocol that partitions a single biological sample into metabolite, protein, and lipid fractions for subsequent multi-omics analyses, typically using mass spectrometry.
A spatial molecular profiling assay that uses mass spectrometry to measure the spatial distribution of molecular analytes within cells or tissues.

An imaging assay that maps the molecular composition of biological samples by detecting inelastic (Raman) scattering of light at each spatial pixel. As a laser scans the sample, each pixel generates a Raman spectrum reflecting the unique molecular vibrational fingerprint of that location, enabling detailed mapping of biomolecules such as proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and water within cells or tissues. The resulting chemical maps provide quantitative, spatially resolved information about tissue composition and molecular organization without the need for staining or fluorescent labels.

A single-cell or single-nucleus sequencing assay that simultaneously measures chromatin accessibility using ATAC sequencing and gene expression using RNA sequencing from the same individual cell or nucleus.

A single-cell or single-nucleus sequencing assay that profiles chromatin accessibility by sequencing DNA fragments generated through transposase-mediated tagging of accessible chromatin in individual cells or nuclei.
A single-cell or single-nucleus sequencing assay that profiles gene expression by sequencing RNA molecules isolated from individual cells or nuclei.

An ATAC sequencing assay that measures genome-wide chromatin accessibility at single-cell resolution. It uniquely uses a split-and-pool \combinatorial indexing\" strategy to barcode individual cells, allowing researchers to profile hundreds of thousands of cells without needing to physically isolate them."
A multimodal single-cell assay that simultaneously measures gene expression by RNA sequencing and protein abundance in the same individual cell.

An imaging assay that produces label-free, highly specific contrast from non-centrosymmetric biological structures—most notably fibrillar collagen. When pulsed laser light interacts with ordered molecular assemblies such as collagen fibrils, photons at exactly half the excitation wavelength are coherently emitted, providing structural specificity without the use of exogenous labels or stains. SHG microscopy enables high-resolution, label-free imaging of extracellular matrix architecture and collagen fiber organization in biological tissues.

A spatial transcriptomics assay that uses solid-phase amplification of randomly barcoded single-molecule oligonucleotides on an Illumina sequencing platform to create a dense array of spatially indexed RNA-capture clusters. Tissue sections are placed directly on the sequencing flow cell surface, where RNA molecules are captured by barcoded clusters and sequenced together with their spatial coordinates. With pixels spaced approximately 0.5–0.8 µm apart, Seq-Scope achieves spatial resolution approaching that of individual cells and subcellular compartments.

An assay that characterizes the elemental and molecular composition of solid surfaces and thin films by bombarding the specimen with a focused primary ion beam, causing secondary ions to be sputtered from the surface and detected by a mass spectrometer. By rastering the primary beam across the sample, SIMS generates spatially resolved chemical maps of isotope distributions, elements, and molecular species at high sensitivity and depth resolution. In biological research, SIMS is used for imaging stable isotope tracers, lipid distributions, and subcellular elemental composition within tissue sections.
A mass spectrometry assay that measures proteins, metabolites, and lipids in individual cells.

A spatial transcriptomics assay that captures RNA expression across tissue sections at single-cell to subcellular resolution over a wide field of view. RNA molecules are captured in situ on a patterned chip containing spatially indexed DNA nanoballs (DNBs)—each assigned a unique Coordinate ID (CID)—enabling precise spatial mapping of transcripts from fresh-frozen tissue. The resulting data supports multi-scale analysis of tissue biology, from tissue-level organization to single-cell gene expression and subcellular transcript localization.

A spatial molecular profiling assay that maps the expression of targeted RNA panels within intact tissue sections at single-cell and subcellular resolution. This assay can identify the location of target transcripts within the tissue, providing a single cell resolution map of expression patterns of all genes that are included in the selected probe panel and generating a single-cell-resolution expression map of all profiled genes.

A spatial transcriptomics assay that maps genome-wide RNA expression in fresh-frozen tissue at submicron resolution. RNA molecules are captured in situ on a barcoded slide surface using spatially indexed poly(d)T oligonucleotides spaced ~0.5 µm apart, then sequenced to reconstruct high-resolution transcriptomic maps. This technology achieves spatial resolution approaching that of a light microscope, enabling near-single-cell or subcellular-level gene expression profiling across intact tissue sections.

A spatial transcriptomics and multiomics assay that uses polony gel arrays—micron-scale DNA cluster arrays each carrying unique spatial barcodes—to capture and sequence RNA, proteins, or other molecules directly from tissue sections. Molecules from the overlaid tissue are captured by the barcoded clusters and spatially indexed according to each cluster's coordinates, enabling high-resolution reconstruction of molecular spatial organization after sequencing.

An imaging assay that applies multiplexed fluorescence microscopy to thick tissue sections using multiphoton excitation, enabling simultaneous or sequential visualization of a large number of cellular and histological protein markers in 3D. Multiphoton excitation allows imaging deep into intact thick sections with reduced phototoxicity and superior optical sectioning compared to single-photon methods.

A spatial molecular profiling assay that profiles RNA expression, protein abundance, and tissue morphology (via fluorescence H&E staining) at subcellular resolution directly from FFPE tissue sections.
A measurement of sleep apnea severity calculated as the total number of apnea and hypopnea events recorded during a sleep study, divided by the total number of hours of sleep.
A self-reported categorical measurement of an individual's cigarette smoking history, classified as current smoker, former smoker, or never smoker.
A unique identifier for the physical glass slide or cartridge on which a tissue section is mounted and processed.

The 10x microfluidic assay that simultaneously profiles the transcriptome and epigenome of the same individual cell nucleus, using a redesigned chip architecture to improve cell partitioning and overall performance in sensitivity, throughput, and data quality.
The 10x assay that simultaneously profiles the transcriptome and epigenome of the same individual cell nucleus, using the first iteration of the microfluidic chip and reagents.
A neuropathologic finding characterised by loss of myelinated axons and associated tissue attenuation in the cerebral white matter, observed on post-mortem histopathologic examination.
Quantification of the severity of rarefaction, comprising loss of myelin, tissue attenuation and reactive astrogliosis, in the cerebral white matter.

A deficiency of the essential metal Zinc; an essential cofactor for many enzymes. Zinc deficiency is caused by a lack of zinc in the diet, loss of zinc after absorption, for example through loss through burns, inability to absorb Zinc, or increased loss through exercise.

Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5), also known as Rienhoff (pronounced REENhoff) syndrome, is characterized by syndromic presentation of aortic aneurysms involving the thoracic and/or abdominal aorta, with risk of dissection and rupture. Other systemic features include cleft palate, bifid uvula, mitral valve disease, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability, and clubfoot deformity; however, not all clinical features occur in all patients. In contrast to other forms of LDS, no striking aortic or arterial tortuosity is present in these patients, and there is no strong evidence for early aortic dissection.

?xrefs: ICD9:413.1 MedDRA:10011088 NCIt:C66915 SNOMEDCT:23687008 SNOMEDCT:87343002 Wikipedia:Prinzmetal's_angina

?def: An abnormally high acidity of the blood and other body tissues. Acidosis can be either respiratory or metabolic
?xrefs: ICD9:276.2 MESH:D000138 MedDRA:10000486 NCIt:C83504 SNOMEDCT:51387008 UMLS:C0001122

?def: An adenoma of the adrenal cortex that produces aldosterone. It may be associated with Conn syndrome. Clinical presentation includes hypertension, hypokalemia, and muscle weakness.
?xrefs: EFO:1000015 ICD10:C74.0 ICD10:E26.0 MedDRA:10056950 NCIT:C48451 Orphanet:231625 UMLS:C1706762 UMLS:CN226945

?def: A poorly differentiated non-small cell lung carcinoma composed of large polygonal cells without evidence of glandular or squamous differentiation
An autosomal recessive disorder means two copies of an abnormal gene must be present in order for the disease or trait to develop.
A synovial sarcoma (disease) that involves the breast.
A carcinoma that arises from glandular epithelial cells of the caecum
A carcinoma that arises from epithelial cells of the caecum
Recurrent infections of the urinary bladder
?xrefs: DOID:1680 ICD9CM:595.2 MedDRA:10008852 NCIt:C27008 SNOMEDCT:33655002 UMLS:C0221763

?def: Chronic rhinosinusitis is a heterogeneous disease characterized by local inflammation of the upper airways and sinuses which persists for at least 12 weeks
An acute or chronic inflammatory process affecting the bladder.
?xrefs: DOID:1679 ICD10:N30 ICD9:595 MESH:D003556 MedDRA:10011781 MedDRA:10011802 NCIt:C26738 SNOMEDCT:38822007 UMLS:C0010692

?def: A neuroglial tumor that arises from the middle portion of the brain stem. It usually affects children and has a poor prognosis.
?xrefs: EFO:1000026 GARD:0013075 NCIT:C94764 ONCOTREE:DIPG Orphanet:497188 UMLS:C2986658

?def: A group of neoplasms which arise from the ependymal lining of the cerebral ventricles and from the remnants of the central canal of the spinal cord. Ependymal tumors occur predominantly in children and young adults with varied morphological features and biological behavior. There are 4 types: ependymoma, anaplastic ependymoma, myxopapillary ependymoma and subependymoma. (WHO)
?xrefs: EFO:1000027 ICD10:C71.7 NCIT:C6770 ONCOTREE:EPMT Orphanet:301 UMLS:C1333407 UMLS:CN203416

?def: A WHO grade II, slow growing tumor of children and young adults, usually located intraventricularly. It is the most common ependymal neoplasm. It often causes clinical symptoms by blocking cerebrospinal fluid pathways. Key histological features include perivascular pseudorosettes and ependymal rosettes. (WHO)
?xrefs: DOID:4844 GARD:0006353 ICD10:D43.2 ICDO:9391/3 MESH:D004806 MedDRA:10014967 NCIT:C3017 ONCOTREE:EPM Orphanet:251636 UMLS:C0014474 UMLS:CN201941

?def: A carcinoma that arises from the stomach and is characterized by the presence of malignant cells with glandular and squamous differentiation.
A variant of gastric adenocarcinoma characterized by prominent dilated or slit-like tubules.

A slow-growing, malignant tumor, characterize by the presence of granulosa-like cells and Call-Exner bodies, that is almost always found in the ovary. In rare cases, it has also been found in the testicle. There are two types of granulosa cell tumor that can be distinguished under the microscope: the adult and the juvenile. The testicular juvenile granulosa cell tumors are perhaps the most common congenital testicular neoplasms.
?xrefs: DOID:2999 EFO:1000032 MESH:D006106 NCIT:C3070 ONCOTREE:GRCT UMLS:C0018206

?def: An autosomal recessive disease characterized by multiple fetal developmental defects including polydactyly and central nervous system malformations that results from a single amino acid mutation of D211G of the HYLS1 gene which plays a central role in cilia formation
It describes patients in whom a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease cannot be made based on standard clinical testing, including colonoscopy, imaging, laboratory tests, and biopsy.
A viral or bacterial infectious process affecting the large intestine

?xrefs: DOID:3650 MESH:D000140 MedDRA:10023676 NCIt:C98969 SNOMEDCT:91273001 UMLS:C0001125

?def: A neuroendocrine neoplasm that arises from the lung. It is characterized by the presence of uniform polygonal cells with small or moderate amount of cytoplasm and inconspicuous nucleoli. The cells are usually arranged in organoid and trabecular patterns. It is classified as typical or atypical carcinoid tumor based on the number of mitotic figures and the absence or presence of necrosis. Atypical carcinoid tumors have a worse prognosis.
A lung carcinoma characterized by the presence of malignant non-keratinizing squamoid cells, mucin-producing cells and intermediate type cells
A bacterial infection of the membranes covering the brain and the spinal cord caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis

A group of invasive breast carcinomas characterized by the presence of an adenocarcinomatous component which is admixed with a dominant component that is composed of squamous cells, spindle cells, or mesenchymal cells.
?xrefs: DOID:4680 EFO:1000040 GARD:0010804 ICD10:C50.0 ICD10:C50.1 ICD10:C50.2 ICD10:C50.3 ICD10:C50.4 ICD10:C50.5 ICD10:C50.6 ICD10:C50.8 NCIT:C5164 ONCOTREE:MBC Orphanet:213531 SCTID:763479005 UMLS:C1334708

?def: Hardening of the walls of the small arteries and arterioles (small arteries that convey blood from arteries to the even smaller capillaries) of the kidney. This condition is caused by hypertension (high blood pressure)
?xrefs: DOID:11664 ICD9:587 MESH:D009400 MedDRA:10029159 SNOMEDCT:32916005 UMLS:C0027719

?def: A malignant glandular epithelial neoplasm characterized by the presence of clear and hobnail cells. It is highly associated with ovarian endometriosis, pelvic endometriosis and paraendocrine hypercalcemia.
?xrefs: DOID:5304 EFO:1000042 ICD10:C56 NCIT:C40078 Orphanet:398971 SCTID:763131005 UMLS:C1518693 UMLS:CN205034

?def: A malignant serous cystic epithelial neoplasm arising from the ovary. It is characterized by the presence of glandular, papillary, or solid structures. Psammoma bodies may be present. In well differentiated cases the malignant epithelial cells resemble the cells of fallopian tube epithelium. In poorly differentiated cases the malignant epithelial cells show anaplastic features.
A carcinoma that arises from glandular epithelial cells of the pancreas
?xrefs: DOID:4074 EFO:1000044 NCIT:C8294 ONCOTREE:PAAD SCTID:700423003 UMLS:C0281361

?def: A low or intermediate grade well differentiated tumor with neuroendocrine differentiation that arises from the pancreas. According to the presence or absence of clinical syndromes that result from hormone hypersecretion, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are classified either as functional or nonfunctional
A morphologic variant of lung adenocarcinoma characterized by the presence of papillary structures.

A rare, aggressive, high grade invasive ductal carcinoma, not otherwise specified. It is characterized by the presence of pleomorphic and bizarre malignant cells that constitute more than 50 percent of the malignant cellular infiltrate.
Pig disease caused by porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2). Most representative symptoms include wasting, unthriftness, paleness of the skin, respiratory distress, diarrhea and sometimes icterus.

A bacterial infection that affects the lungs and is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Most patients with tuberculosis do not have symptoms (latent tuberculosis) and are not contagious. When signs and symptoms occur (active tuberculosis), patients become contagious. The signs and symptoms include chronic cough with blood-tinged sputum, night sweats, fever, fatigue, and weight loss
?xrefs: DOID:2957 ICD10:A15 ICD10:A16 ICD9:011 MESH:D014397 MedDRA:10037440 MedDRA:10037443 NCIt:C26899 SNOMEDCT:154283005 UMLS:C0041327

?def: A leiomyoma that involves the kidney.
A benign or malignant, primary or metastatic neoplasm affecting the male and female reproductive system.
A rare carcinoma that arises from the breast parenchyma and is entirely composed of squamous cells.
A lymphoma that arises from the thymus. Representative examples include mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma.

A squamous cell carcinoma that arises from the tongue. It usually presents as a painful ulcerated or nodular lesion. The size of the tumor and the status of the lymph nodes are the most important factors that determine prognosis.

An embryonal neoplasm characterized by the presence of epithelial, mesenchymal, and blastema components. The vast majority of cases arise from the kidney. A small number of cases with morphologic features resembling Wilms tumor of the kidney have been reported arising from the ovary and the cervix
A squamous cell carcinoma that arises from the nasal cavity mucosa. Signs and symptoms include nasal fullness and obstruction, pain, epistaxis, and the presence of a nasal mass.
A squamous cell carcinoma that arises from the nasopharynx.

a tear within the wall of any of the arteries of the neck (carotid artery or vertebral artery) and that allows blood to separate the wall layers. By separating a portion of the wall of the artery (a layer of the Tunica intima or tunica media), a dissection creates two lumens or passages within the vessel, the native or true lumen, and the \false lumen\" created by the new space within the wall of the artery."

Inherited or acquired disorders of sugar metabolism. Deficiencies of lactase, maltase or sucrase-isomaltase usually occur irreversibly and independent of one another. Congenital deficiencies are rare whereas acquired deficiencies are more common and may be seen following intestinal mucosal brush-border injury. Clinical signs include abdominal cramping, bloating, flatulence and diarrhea following dietary intake of lactose, maltose or sucrose. The clinical course leads to malabsorption of disaccharides which has implications for normal growth and development if manifested at an early age.

Inability to fully digest and absorb lactose due to limited or no lactase activity in the small intestine. Congenital intolerance is inherited following an autosomal recessive pattern but is rare. It is more often due to a gradual decline of lactase production in adulthood following the ingestion of fewer lactose-containing foods or secondary to an intestinal mucosal brush-border injury. Prevalence is highest among Asians, Native Americans and Africans. Clinical signs include abdominal cramping, bloating, flatulence and diarrhea following the dietary intake of lactose.
Adult onset lactose intolerance
A variant of acinar prostate adenocarcinoma characterized by the presence of malignant cells with abundant xanthomatous appearing cytoplasm.

A usually aggressive morphologic variant of acinar adenocarcinoma of the prostate gland characterized by the presence of lakes of extracellular mucin. This diagnosis applies when at least 25% of the resected tumor contains extracellular mucin.

An adenoma of the pituitary gland that produces corticotropin. The vast majority of cases are associated with Cushing disease. Clinical manifestations include truncal obesity with thin extremities, thinning of the skin, osteoporosis, and a tendency to bruise easily. Silent or hormonally non-functioning ACTH producing adenomas have also been described. They produce symptoms of a mass-related lesion.
A rare, hormonally functioning or non-functioning pituitary gland adenocarcinoma that produces corticotropin. It may be associated with Cushing disease.

A clonal (malignant) hematopoietic disorder with an acute onset, affecting the bone marrow and the peripheral blood. The malignant cells show minimal differentiation and are called blasts, either myeloid blasts (myeloblasts) or lymphoid blasts (lymphoblasts).

A craniopharyngioma consisting of broad strands, cords and bridges of a multistratified squamous epithelium with peripheral palisading of nuclei. Diagnostic features include nodules of compact 'wet' keratin and dystrophic calcification. (Adapted from WHO)

A benign neoplasm characterized by the presence of connective tissue stroma and epithelial structures. It occurs in the ovary, fallopian tube, uterine corpus, and cervix. Cases of adenofibroma of the ovary with low grade malignant potential have also been reported.
An adenoid cystic carcinoma primarily involving the breast. Three morphologic patterns are seen: cribriform, trabecular, and solid. The prognosis is excellent.

A benign, slow growing neoplasm arising from tooth-forming tissues. The vast majority of cases are intraosseous and most often grow in the maxilla. It is characterized by the presence of odontogenic epithelium which is embedded in a connective tissue stroma. Local excision is curative and recurrences are very rare.
A carcinoma composed of malignant glandular cells and malignant squamous cells.
A benign soft tissue lesion arising from the adrenal gland. It is composed of mature adipose and hematopoietic/lymphoid tissues.
A neuroblastoma arising from the adrenal gland.
